## Understanding Passenger Side SRS Connectors in GM Vehicles

When looking under the seat of a Chevrolet Aveo from the mid-2000s, seeing two thick yellow connectors on the passenger side can be confusing if you are only familiar with standard driver-side configurations. On the driver's side, it is common to see one primary connector for the Supplemental Restraint System (SRS) module and a secondary harness often used for seat belt sensors or occupancy detection. However, the passenger side typically presents two identical-looking yellow plugs that both route into the seat cushion.

The first cable in this pair is undeniably the SRS driver circuit. This heavy-gauge wire carries high-current signals from the airbag module to the inflator and includes a pre-charge resistor to stabilize voltage before deployment. The second connector, which appears identical but serves a different function, is almost certainly for the passenger occupant detection system or side-curtain airbag sensor.

In many General Motors platforms of that era, including the Aveo, the front passenger seat utilizes an Occupancy Sensing System (OSS). Unlike simple weight sensors found in older models, these systems often use capacitive sensing technology embedded within the foam of the seat cushion. The system estimates the mass and posture of the occupant to decide whether to deploy the airbag at full force, reduced force, or not at all for rear-facing child seats. If your vehicle has this feature, you will find a second thick yellow harness terminating at the sensor module located inside the passenger seat base.

The fact that your SRS light is illuminated solid red, rather than blinking a diagnostic code pattern, indicates a hard fault in the system. While a dealership suggested replacing the battery as a remedy for an aging 2007 unit, this advice is often a heuristic fallback when specific OBD-II scanners lack the proprietary protocol to read GM SRS codes correctly. A modern battery replacement will not resolve a wiring short, an open circuit in the occupant sensor harness, or a failed internal capacitor within the airbag module itself.

Your attempt to clean the connectors with WD-40 was understandable but technically misaligned with best practices. Contact cleaner should be non-conductive and volatile; WD-40 is primarily a lubricant and corrosion inhibitor that can leave an oily residue, potentially attracting dust or creating erratic resistance in sensitive airbag circuits. For future maintenance, use a dedicated electrical contact cleaner like CRC QD or Brakleen, followed by dry compressed air to ensure no dielectric fluid remains inside the connector housing.

If cleaning does not resolve the issue, the problem likely lies within the seat's internal sensor module or the wiring harness running through the carpet. Since these components are often integrated into the seat structure, diagnosis usually requires removing the seat entirely to inspect for broken wires or checking resistance values with a multimeter against factory schematics. Without access to specific GM SRS diagnostic codes, pinpointing whether the fault is in the detection logic or the deployment circuit remains difficult without specialized equipment.

For developers and engineers working on embedded automotive systems, this scenario highlights the complexity of safety-critical subsystems where redundancy and precise sensing are paramount. If you decide to pursue further diagnostics beyond basic cleaning, ensure you have a multimeter capable of measuring low resistance accurately and consult official service manuals for the specific year and trim level of your Aveo.
